title: Orbital Angular Momentum Currents and Textures in a Multiorbital Double Helix
authors: Danny Cordova, Edwin Vásconez, Ernesto Medina
abstract: The microscopic origin of chirality induced spin selectivity (CISS) in biomolecular structures has traditionally been discussed in terms of spin orbit coupling and spin angular momentum. However, orbital angular momentum (OAM) is increasingly recognized as a more direct electronic response to molecular chirality. A helical hopping network built only from s orbitals can support an itinerant orbital moment and an orbital Edelstein response, but such a basis has no local atomic OAM and therefore omits the complementary contribution arising from coherence among active p orbitals. Here we construct a six-band multiorbital double helix model parameterized by characteristic B form DNA geometry and hopping scales. The model incorporates major minor groove asymmetry, an axial base pair offset representing stagger, and compositional inequivalence between the two strands, providing structural control parameters with which the orbital response can be tuned. Inter strand hybridization generates a full three component atomic OAM texture in the corotating local helical frame, including a radial component absent in the corresponding single helix model. We separately evaluate the itinerant OAM using the Bloch wave packet formulation of orbital magnetization and identify an additional inter-strand circulation channel unique to the double-helix connectivity. The resulting atomic and itinerant responses have distinct microscopic origins, magnitudes, and temperature dependences, establishing a multiorbital framework for geometry controlled angular momentum generation and transport in chiral molecular conductors.
summary: This work develops a multiorbital tight-binding model for a double helix, treating OAM as a key electronic response to molecular chirality. By incorporating inter-strand coupling, the model predicts the emergence of a full 3D atomic OAM texture and a unique radial itinerant OAM current. This establishes a framework for understanding geometry-controlled angular momentum transport in chiral biomolecular systems.
main_problem: The study investigates Orbital Angular Momentum (OAM) as a direct electronic response to molecular chirality, moving beyond traditional spin-orbit coupling descriptions.
main_result: The double-helix structure generates a full three-component atomic OAM texture and a unique radial itinerant OAM component, which are distinct from single-helix contributions.
method: The authors construct and diagonalize a multiorbital, six-band tight-binding Hamiltonian parameterized by B-DNA geometry, analyzing both local atomic and itinerant OAM.
model_or_system: The system is a multiorbital double-helix model, parameterized by B-form DNA geometry, incorporating major-minor groove asymmetry and inter-strand coupling via a $6 	imes 6$ Bloch Hamiltonian.

important_parameters: B-form DNA geometry parameters ($\phi_0, z_0$), hopping scales, and the structural asymmetry that activates cross-couplings.
main_assumptions: The model uses a tight-binding parameterization and neglects explicit spin-orbit coupling, contacts, or dephasing mechanisms in the primary analysis.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the double-helix geometry, the resulting full 3D atomic OAM texture, and the elementary inter-strand plaquette responsible for the radial itinerant OAM.
paper_structure: The paper builds the Hamiltonian using a localized, co-rotating frame, analyzes the full $6 	imes 6$ Bloch matrix, and then separates the analysis into local atomic OAM (from coherence) and itinerant OAM (from plaquette circulation).
why_interesting: The explicit derivation of geometry-controlled, non-zero radial itinerant OAM via inter-strand plaquettes provides a novel topological mechanism for generating orbital polarization in chiral molecular conductors.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic representation of the double helix geom- etry and local orbital basis. The red and blue backbones represent the two helical strands wrapping around the cen- tral z-axis, with radius a and axial rise hz. The structural asymmetry is defined by the minor groove angle φ0 and the major groove angle 2π −φ0 = 210◦, as well as an inter-strand vertical shear z0. Position vectors R1,n and R2,n locate site n on each strand, with d1,n and d12,n representing the intra- strand and inter-strand bond vectors, respectively. At each lattice site, the local electronic states are modeled using pr, pϕ, and pz orbitals.

FIG. 2. Electronic band structure of the fully coupled six- band B-DNA double-helix model. Panel (a) isolates the low- est energy states: ν = 1 (blue), ν = 2 (red), corresponding primarily to the longitudinal pz orbitals. Panel (b) details the remaining higher-energy manifolds: ν = 3 (green), ν = 4 (or- ange), ν = 5 (purple), ν = 6 (cyan), dominated by hybridized transverse modes. The structural and compositional asym- metry lifts the degeneracies of the corresponding symmetric model.

FIG. 3. Momentum-dependent orbital angular momen- tum textures for the six-band double-helix model. The color coding follows the band indexing (ν = 1, . . . , 6) established in Fig. 2. Panels (a), (b), and (c) display the radial, az- imuthal, and longitudinal components, respectively. Time- reversal symmetry imposes the antisymmetric orbital texture ⟨Lα⟩ν(k) = −⟨Lα⟩ν(−k). Crucially, panel (a) demonstrates the emergence of a finite radial orbital texture ⟨Lr⟩ν(k), which is absent in the corresponding isolated single-helix model.

FIG. 4. Temperature dependence of the linear atomic Edel- stein susceptibility χLα at the chemical potentials that max- imize the response. The different components reflect distinct orbital sectors and their thermal sampling near avoided cross- ings. (a) Radial response. (b) Azimuthal response near µ = 1 eV (solid line) and near µ = −1 eV (dashed line). The az- imuthal component is appreciable in two distinct energy win- dows. (c) Longitudinal response.

FIG. 5. Temperature dependence of the second-order orbital current conductivity σ(2) Lα for (a) radial, (b) azimuthal (solid: µ = 1.14 eV, dashed: µ = −0.95 eV), and (c) longitudinal components. As in Fig. 4, the azimuthal conductivity is ap- preciable in two chemical-potential windows.
